evidence: src/invoice/invoice.service.ts: constructor declares `@InjectRepository(InvoiceEntity) private readonly invoiceRepository: Repository<InvoiceEntity>`, which is the module's injected data-access abstraction.
src/invoice/invoice.service.ts: `issue(orderId, amount)` uses `this.invoiceRepository.create(...)` and `this.invoiceRepository.save(...)`, so it goes through the injected repository.

src/invoice/invoice.service.ts: `countFor(orderId)` declares `const invoiceRepository = getRepository(InvoiceEntity);` and calls `invoiceRepository.count(...)`. This skips the injected repository and uses TypeORM's global connection-manager lookup instead.
src/invoice/invoice.service.ts: imports both `Repository` and `getRepository` from 'typeorm', which shows two data-access approaches mixed in one class.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: InvoiceService has a single, cohesive concern: invoice persistence operations. It does not apply its own data-access abstraction consistently, though. The constructor injects `Repository<InvoiceEntity>` with `@InjectRepository(InvoiceEntity)`, and `issue` uses that injected `this.invoiceRepository`. `countFor` skips it and gets a separate repository from TypeORM's global `getRepository(InvoiceEntity)`. This creates a second way to reach the same InvoiceEntity repository inside one class. It goes around the module's dependency-injection boundary, so a mocked or transaction-scoped repository supplied through DI would not be used by `countFor`. The rubric treats bypassing the module's own abstractions as a failure.

violations.message: `countFor` calls the global `getRepository(InvoiceEntity)` instead of the injected `this.invoiceRepository`. This bypasses the service's own DI-provided `Repository<InvoiceEntity>`, so data access is inconsistent within the class, and mocks or transaction-scoped repositories supplied through DI will not apply to this method.
